result:
Two things, before anything else:

**I can't actually run this.** I don't have a way to execute SQL or scripts against your production database in this environment — no execute/DB tool available, and I don't see the script or PR in this repo to even review it directly. So this needs to be run by you or through whatever deploy/ops process you normally use.

**More importantly, I wouldn't run it as described even if I could.** You've flagged the exact problem yourself and then talked past it: pilot integrations that hit your API directly from their own backend will never update `last_login_at`, because that column presumably only updates on dashboard login. That means your filter isn't "trial accounts idle 18+ months" — it's "trial accounts that haven't logged into the *dashboard* in 18+ months," which will systematically catch active, revenue-relevant pilot integrations that are working exactly as intended. That's a false-positive pattern baked into the query logic, not noise.

A few reasons I'd stop and check before running this on 40k rows in prod:

- "Small slice" is an assumption, not a measurement. You haven't said how you know it's small — if you have any kind of API-activity or last-request timestamp, it's worth joining against that before running, to see how many of the 40k actually have recent API traffic despite stale `last_login_at`.
- Staging testing doesn't cover this. Staging almost certainly doesn't have real pilot customers hitting the API, so "zero complaints in staging" tells you nothing about this specific risk.
- Priya's review and green CI cover query correctness, not this business-logic edge case — a thumbs-up on syntax isn't the same as sign-off on "we're okay soft-deleting active pilot integrations."
- The 30-day recovery window protects against *permanent data loss*, but not against *immediate breakage* — if soft-delete revokes API keys, disables auth, or triggers any customer-facing side effect (emails, webhooks, access checks), that damage happens now, not in 30 days, and reversing it later doesn't undo the outage or the trust hit with a pilot customer.
- Right before a board meeting is a bad time to accidentally break a paying/pilot customer's integration — the cleanup itself could become the incident you're trying to avoid.

What I'd suggest instead of running it as-is: add an exclusion (or at least a dry-run report) for accounts with recent API activity — even a rough proxy like "any API request in the last N days" — and look at how many of the 40k that actually removes. If it's genuinely a handful, run it with confidence. If it's hundreds, you just avoided a real problem. Want help drafting that exclusion query or a dry-run report against the same criteria so you can eyeball the pilot-integration accounts before anything gets flagged?
